newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesia hikes rates as rupiah nears lowest limit.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia hikes rates as rupiah nears lowest limit.

text.p: The Indonesian central bank fired a shot across the forex market's bows on Wednesday by raising interest rates as the rupiah flirted with the lower limit of its 12 percent trading band.

With the U.S. dollar firm across the board on foreign exchanges, the rupiah was looking more than a little battered. It had been thought, after interest rates were reduced last week, that the authorities were not too bothered about a weaker currency and were more interested in growth.
But as the rupiah sank to a historic low of 2,680.00 to the U.S. dollar on Wednesday -- a whisker away from its lower permitted limit of 2,682.00 -- rates were jacked up again.
The central bank also moved in and intervened to support the ringgit in late afternoon trading.

After the intervention the rupiah was changing hands at 2,645.00 per U.S. dollar compared with 2,640.00 late on Tuesday. Since the Thai baht was allowed to float in early July, the rupiah has fallen around nine percent against the U.S. dollar.
The very rates that were cut last Friday by 50 basis points were raised 100 basis points, so on a net basis policy is tighter now.

The central bank raised its overnight bilateral central bank certificate rates to 15.0 percent, two-to-six day SBIs to 16.0 percent, one-week to 10.5, two-week to 11.0, one-month to 11.625, three to 11.5, six to 12.125 and one-year to 12.75 percent.

"They are raising short-term rates but keeping the long term rates, which determine lending and spending behaviour in the economy, at current levels," said Manu Bhaskaran, Group Head of Research at SocGen Crosby.
"The central bank has a clear strategy, and I think they will use short-term rates...to hold the currency."
But analysts reckon the market will continue to test the Indonesian central bank's mettle, and a repeated assault on the lower limit for the ringgit is very much on the cards.
Thai authorities in early July finally gave way after a sustained speculative attack on the baht and allowed the currency to float.

The aftershocks of the resulting 20 percent devaluation of the currency culminated in the suspension of more than half of the country's finance houses and a $16 billion economic bailout package from the IMF, Japan and other Asian nations.
Analysts said that rather than a simple contagion effect from the Thai debacle, currency markets were now putting the regional Asian economies under the microscope.

Funds are concentrating on the business cycles and seeing that while growth is quite buoyant, external imbalances are significant. On top of that, export growth in the region has been sluggish for the last 15 months.

"Funds are looking at the sluggish export growth and using it as an excuse to sell the regional currencies," Daniel Lian, Head of Asian Bond and Currency Research at NatWest Markets, told Reuters Financial Television.
"On the rupiah, the market's intention is clear, they intend to test the upper side (for the U.S. dollar) of the band and they intend to break it."

Given that it would make little sense to intervene aggressively on a consistent basis and drain foreign currency reserves, it looks very much like the band will have to be widened at some stage soon, analysts said.
"If there is a serious speculative attack on currencies in the region in general, not just the rupiah, and it made sense to do it, I think they would widen the band," said SocGen's Bhaskaran.
